# An Algebra of Prediction-Rewarding Mechanisms

### Scoring Rules, Market Makers, and Opinion Pools Generated by One Convex Function

Peter Cotton · Microprediction · peter.cotton@microprediction.com · *Working draft v0.5* · 2026

---

## Abstract

Scoring rules, cost-function market makers, and opinion pools are taught as
separate subjects with separate notation. All three are generated by one
convex function of the forecast. A proper scoring rule is that function read
at the report, a cost-function market maker is its Fenchel conjugate, and the
linear and logarithmic opinion pools are the two Kullback-Leibler barycenters.
Merging two market makers is infimal convolution, so liquidity adds. The
mechanisms are given one input-output signature so that they can be chained,
and several familiar statistical methods, Bayesian model averaging, least
squares, the Kalman filter and split-conformal prediction, are then chains
with one degree of freedom frozen. Every statement is worked on a single
three-outcome example.

---

## 1. Introduction

Consider an organiser who wants a probability forecast for an event with
three outcomes and has three ways to pay for it. She can pay each forecaster
by a scoring rule, a fixed formula of the reported probabilities and the
outcome. She can open a market in which forecasters buy and sell shares that
pay one unit if an outcome occurs, and read the forecast off the prices. Or
she can collect the forecasts and average them. The three designs have three
literatures.

They are one subject. Fix a convex function $G$ on the set of probability
vectors. Reading $G$ and its slope at the reported probabilities gives a
proper scoring rule, and every proper scoring rule arises this way (Theorem
1). Taking the convex conjugate of $G$ gives the cost function of an
automated market maker, whose prices, freedom from arbitrage, and worst-case
loss are three properties of the conjugate (Theorem 2). Averaging forecasts
has two natural senses, and they are the two minimisers of a
Kullback-Leibler divergence taken in its two directions (Proposition 4).

Results transfer in both directions. The gap between a truthful report and a
false one under a proper score is a Bregman divergence, and the same
function bounds what the corresponding market maker can lose. Two market
makers run side by side behave as one deeper maker, with the depth adding,
because conjugation turns a sum of convex functions into an infimal
convolution (Proposition 5).

Once the mechanisms are written in one signature, several familiar
statistical procedures appear as the same mechanisms with a degree of
freedom frozen. Bayesian model averaging is a market of Kelly bettors with
entry closed. Weighted least squares is a merge of quadratic makers with
their capital fixed. Split-conformal prediction is a two-stage chain whose
residual stage admits one unconditional entry, and the freeze forfeits a
rent with a closed form, the mutual information between residual and input.

Deployed systems use little of this. Numerai pooled staked submissions into
one stake-weighted meta-model and paid each forecast its marginal
contribution [@craib2017numeraire]. CrunchDAO blends each contest into one
ensemble. The IARPA prediction polls aggregated forecasts by track record and
compared favourably with head-to-head markets [@atanasov2017distilling]. In
every case there is one pool and one internal aggregate, and the mechanism is
chosen by convention rather than by the function that generates it.

The mechanisms also chain. The forecast one stage emits can be the message
the next stage scores, or the coordinate in which the next stage settles.
Chaining requires every mechanism to consume and emit the same kind of
object, a distribution, and the mechanisms are written that way. The
multi-stage theory and its deployment on the microprediction platform are
treated in a companion report [@cotton2026multistage]. Two related results
are treated elsewhere: elicitation from finite point clouds
[@cotton2026pointcloud] and the parimutuel account of a conformal
predictor's information gap [@cotton2026conformalbetting].

The running example has outcomes $A$, $B$ and $C$. The forecaster's belief is $q=(0.5,0.3,0.2)$, the false report under
consideration is $p=(0.7,0.2,0.1)$, and the market maker, where there is one,
has liquidity $b=10$. Numbers are rounded to two or three places.

## 2. Scoring rules and the convex toolkit

**The finite setting.** Outcomes are a finite set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a
forecast is a vector $p$ in the probability simplex $\Delta$, with
non-negative entries summing to one. In the running example $n=3$. The
continuous setting, densities on $\mathbb R$ or $[0,1]^d$, is needed for the
opinion pools and the probability integral transform. The finite statements
transfer with the usual measure-theoretic care, except where noted.

**Scoring rules.** A scoring rule pays $S(p,i)\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}$ to
a forecaster who reported $p$ when outcome $i$ occurs. Higher is better. A
forecaster who believes $q$ and reports $p$ expects to receive
$S(p;q)=\sum_i q_i S(p,i)$, assumed well defined with $S(q;q)$ finite. The
rule is *proper* if $S(q;q)\ge S(p;q)$ for all $p,q$: reporting one's belief
is never worse than misreporting. It is *strictly proper* if equality forces
$p=q$, so that the truth is the only optimal report.

The logarithmic score $S(p,i)=\log p_i$ is the standard example
[@good1952rational]. In the running example the truthful report expects
$\sum_i q_i\log q_i=-1.030$ and the false report expects
$\sum_i q_i\log p_i=-1.122$. Misreporting costs $0.092$ in expectation, and
the number is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between $q$ and $p$.

**Convex functions and the Bregman divergence.** A function $G$ on $\Delta$
is convex when the chord between any two points of its graph lies above the
graph. Its slope at $p$ is a vector $G'(p)$ in the subdifferential
$\partial G(p)$, the set of slopes of hyperplanes that touch the graph at $p$
and lie below it everywhere. For differentiable $G$ there is one such slope,
the gradient. The *Bregman divergence*

$$D_G(q,p)=G(q)-G(p)-\langle G'(p),q-p\rangle$$

is the height of the graph at $q$ above the tangent plane drawn at $p$. It is
non-negative because the tangent plane lies below a convex graph, and it is
zero only at $q=p$ when $G$ is strictly convex. For $G(p)=\sum_i p_i\log p_i$
the divergence is the Kullback-Leibler divergence
$\mathrm{KL}(q\Vert p)=\sum_i q_i\log(q_i/p_i)$, which in the running
example is $0.092$.

**The conjugate.** The Legendre-Fenchel conjugate of a function $R$ on
$\Delta$ is

$$R^*(\mathbf q)=\sup_{p\in\Delta}\ \langle p,\mathbf q\rangle-R(p),
\qquad \mathbf q\in\mathbb R^n.$$

For each vector $\mathbf q$ the conjugate finds the probability vector $p$
that best trades the linear reward $\langle p,\mathbf q\rangle$ against the
penalty $R(p)$, and records the best value. In the market reading, $\mathbf q$ is the vector of outstanding shares and the maximiser is the
price vector.

**Infimal convolution and conventions.** The infimal convolution of $f$ and
$g$ is $(f\,\square\,g)(x)=\inf_y f(y)+g(x-y)$, the cheapest way to split
$x$ into a part handled by $f$ and a part handled by $g$. Conjugation turns
sums into infimal convolutions, which is the content of Proposition 5.
"Closed proper convex" is used in the standard sense
[@rockafellar1970convex]. Differentiable statements are on the relative
interior of $\Delta$, with extended-real values allowed on the boundary, and
subgradients on $\Delta$ act on its tangent space and are defined up to
multiples of $\mathbf 1$.

## 3. Proper scoring rules are convex functions

The organiser wants the forecaster's belief, not a report tuned to the
payment formula. Suppose she pays $p_i$ when outcome $i$ occurs. A
forecaster with belief $q$ then expects $\sum_i q_i p_i$, which is largest
when all the mass is placed on the most likely outcome. The payment has
elicited a mode, not a distribution. Properness rules this out, and Theorem
1 says that properness is convexity.

**Theorem 1 (a scoring rule is proper exactly when it is a convex function
read at the report; @savage1971elicitation, @mccarthy1956measures).** *A
regular scoring rule $S$ is proper iff there is a convex
$G:\Delta\to\mathbb R$ with*

$$S(p,i) \;=\; G(p) + \langle\, G'(p),\; e_i - p\,\rangle,
\qquad G'(p)\in\partial G(p)\quad(p\in\operatorname{ri}\Delta),$$

*where $e_i$ is the $i$-th unit vector. It is strictly proper iff $G$ is
strictly convex relative to $\Delta$, and then $G(p)=S(p;p)$ is the expected
score of a truthful forecaster.*

The display says that the payment on outcome $i$ is the tangent plane of $G$
at the report, evaluated at the vertex $e_i$. The expected payment under
belief $q$ is therefore the tangent plane evaluated at $q$, which lies below
$G(q)$ by exactly the Bregman divergence $D_G(q,p)$. Truth-telling gains
$D_G(q,p)\ge0$, and strict convexity makes the gain positive for every
$p\neq q$.

**Proof.** ($\Leftarrow$) Since $\sum_i q_i(e_i-p)=q-p$, the expected score
is affine in the belief: $S(p;q)=G(p)+\langle G'(p),q-p\rangle$. Hence

$$S(q;q)-S(p;q) \;=\; G(q)-G(p)-\langle G'(p),\,q-p\rangle \;=\; D_G(q,p),$$

which is non-negative by the supporting-hyperplane inequality, and zero only
at $q=p$ when $G$ is strictly convex relative to $\Delta$; so $S$ is
(strictly) proper.

($\Rightarrow$) Define $G(q):=S(q;q)$. Properness says
$G(q)=\sup_p S(p;q)$, and each $q\mapsto S(p;q)=\langle S(p,\cdot),q\rangle$
is affine, so $G$ is a pointwise supremum of affine functions, hence convex.
For any fixed $p$,

$$S(p;q) \;=\; G(p) + \langle S(p,\cdot),\, q-p\rangle
\quad\text{with}\quad S(p;q)\le G(q)\ \ \forall q,$$

so the vector $S(p,\cdot)$ is a subgradient of $G$ at $p$ (acting on the
tangent space of $\Delta$, where subgradients are defined up to a constant
shift along $\mathbf 1$, which the representation absorbs). Substituting
$G'(p)=S(p,\cdot)$ into the display returns $S(p,i)$ identically. For
strictness, note $D_G(q,p)=0$ exactly when $G$ has a supporting hyperplane at
$p$ that also supports $G$ at $q$. If $G$ carried a nontrivial affine segment
in $\Delta$, a hyperplane supporting it at an interior point of the segment
would support it along the whole segment, giving $D_G(q,p)=0$ for a distinct
$q\neq p$, so $S$ would not be strictly proper; conversely strict convexity
relative to $\Delta$ forces $D_G(q,p)=0$ only at $q=p$. $\blacksquare$

Theorem 1 is the dictionary *proper scoring rule $\leftrightarrow$ convex
function $\leftrightarrow$ Bregman divergence*
[@gneiting2007strictly; @banerjee2005optimality]. The three classical scores
are three choices of $G$, with the divergences computed directly from the
definition:

| Score | Generator $G(p)=S(p;p)$ | Bregman divergence $D_G(q,p)$ |
|--------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------------|
| logarithmic | $\sum_i p_i\log p_i$ | $\mathrm{KL}(q\Vert p)$ |
| Brier (quadratic) | $\lVert p\rVert_2^2$ | $\lVert q-p\rVert_2^2$ |
| spherical | $\lVert p\rVert_2$ | $\lVert q\rVert_2\,(1-\cos\theta_{p,q})$ |

For the logarithmic row the representation gives $S(p,i)=\log p_i$ on the
relative interior, with $-\infty$ on the boundary. For the Brier row
[@brier1950verification] it gives $S(p,i)=2p_i-\lVert p\rVert^2$. For the
spherical row, $\nabla G(p)=p/\lVert p\rVert$, so
$D_G(q,p)=\lVert q\rVert-\langle p,q\rangle/\lVert p\rVert
=\lVert q\rVert(1-\cos\theta_{p,q})$, an angular term scaled by
$\lVert q\rVert$.

In the running example the Brier score pays $0.86$, $-0.14$ and $-0.34$ on
the three outcomes for the false report $p=(0.7,0.2,0.1)$. The truthful
report expects $0.38$ and the false report expects $0.32$, so the gap is
$0.06=\lVert q-p\rVert^2$. Under the logarithmic score the same misreport
cost $0.092$. The two rules penalise the same lie by different amounts, and
the difference is entirely the choice of $G$.

## 4. The same function runs a market

A scoring rule pays one forecaster for one report. A market lets many
participants arrive at different times, correct one another, and be paid in
proportion to how much each improved the forecast. The automated version is
the *cost-function market maker* [@hanson2003combinatorial;
@hanson2007logarithmic]. The maker sells shares in each outcome, a share
paying one unit if that outcome occurs, and quotes the price of any bundle
from a fixed convex function $C$ of its outstanding inventory $\mathbf q$: a
trader who moves the inventory from $\mathbf q$ to $\mathbf q'$ pays
$C(\mathbf q')-C(\mathbf q)$. There is no counterparty search and no empty
order book, because the maker always quotes.

Hanson's logarithmic market scoring rule (LMSR) is the case
$C(\mathbf q)=b\log\sum_i e^{q_i/b}$. In the running example the maker
starts with no shares outstanding and quotes each outcome at $1/3$. A trader
buys $10$ shares of $A$ and pays $C(10,0,0)-C(0,0,0)=4.53$; the prices move
to $(0.576,0.212,0.212)$. A second trader buys $5$ shares of $B$ for $1.29$,
and the prices become $(0.506,0.307,0.186)$. Had the first trader sold her
ten shares straight back, she would have received exactly $4.53$: costs
telescope along any path of trades, so a round trip costs nothing.

If $A$ occurs after the first trade, the maker has collected $4.53$ and pays
out $10$, a loss of $5.47$. Theorem 2 bounds the loss over every possible
sequence of trades by $b\log 3=10.99$. The maker's capital at risk is set by
$b$, and $b$ also sets how far a trade of a given size moves the price.

The LMSR is the logarithmic score run sequentially. Writing $p_i(\mathbf q)$
for the price of outcome $i$, the inventory satisfies
$q_i=b\log p_i(\mathbf q)+C(\mathbf q)$, so a trader who moves the prices
from $p$ to $p'$ and then sees outcome $i$ nets
$b\,(\log p'_i-\log p_i)$. The first trader in the example moved the price
of $A$ from $0.333$ to $0.576$ and, when $A$ occurs, collects
$10\,(\log 0.576-\log 0.333)=5.47$. Each participant is paid the improvement
in the log score between the prices they found and the prices they left,
scaled by $b$.

Theorem 2 says that every proper scoring rule has such a market, obtained by
reading its generator $G$ as a penalty and taking the conjugate. The market's
prices, its freedom from arbitrage, and its worst-case loss are then three
properties of the conjugate.

**Theorem 2 (the conjugate of a proper score is an arbitrage-free market
maker with bounded loss; @hanson2007logarithmic, @abernethy2013efficient).**
*Let $R$ be closed, proper, strictly convex, and finite-valued on $\Delta$
(in particular $R(e_i)<\infty$ at every vertex, which the worst-case-loss
bound needs), extended by $+\infty$ off $\Delta$ so that $C=R^*$ below is the
Fenchel conjugate on $\mathbb R^n$, and define*

$$C(\mathbf q)=\sup_{p\in\Delta}\big(\langle p,\mathbf q\rangle - R(p)\big).$$

*Then:*

*(i) $C$ is convex and finite, the maximiser $p^\ast(\mathbf q)$ is unique,
and $\nabla C(\mathbf q)=p^\ast(\mathbf q)\in\Delta$: prices are a probability
vector. (Without strict convexity, prices lie in $\partial C(\mathbf q)$.)*

*(ii) $C$ is translation-equivariant, $C(\mathbf q+\alpha\mathbf 1)
=C(\mathbf q)+\alpha$; costs telescope over any trade path, so round trips
cost zero and buying the full bundle costs its payout: the market is
arbitrage-free.*

*(iii) With initial state $\mathbf q_0=\mathbf 0$, the maker's loss when the
market settles on outcome $i$ after net sales $\mathbf q$ is*

$$\mathrm{loss}_i(\mathbf q) = q_i - C(\mathbf q) + C(\mathbf 0)
\;\le\; R(e_i) - \inf_{p\in\Delta} R(p)
\;\le\; \sup_{p\in\Delta} R(p) - \inf_{p\in\Delta} R(p).$$

*(iv) Taking $R(p)=b\sum_i p_i\log p_i$ gives
$C(\mathbf q)=b\log\sum_i e^{q_i/b}$, Hanson's LMSR, with worst-case loss
$b\log n$.*

Take $R=G$, the generator of Theorem 1 read as a penalty. Prices
are the gradient of the conjugate (Danskin's theorem), no-arbitrage is its
translation-equivariance, and the loss bound is the range of the penalty
over the simplex (Fenchel-Moreau). For the LMSR the penalty is
$b\sum_i p_i\log p_i$, which is $0$ at a vertex and $-b\log n$ at the
uniform distribution, so the range is $b\log n$.

**Proof.** (i) $C$ is a supremum of affine functions of $\mathbf q$, hence
convex; the supremum of a continuous function over the compact $\Delta$ is
attained, and strict concavity of
$p\mapsto\langle p,\mathbf q\rangle-R(p)$ makes the maximiser unique.
Danskin's theorem gives $\nabla C(\mathbf q)=p^\ast(\mathbf q)$.

(ii) $\langle p,\mathbf q+\alpha\mathbf 1\rangle
=\langle p,\mathbf q\rangle+\alpha$ for $p\in\Delta$, so the supremum shifts
by $\alpha$. A trader moving the state $\mathbf q\to\mathbf q'$ pays
$C(\mathbf q')-C(\mathbf q)$ by definition, so costs over any path telescope;
a round trip costs zero, and by translation equivariance the bundle
$\alpha\mathbf 1$ costs exactly $\alpha$, its sure payout.

(iii) The maker collects $C(\mathbf q)-C(\mathbf 0)$ and pays $q_i$, so
$\mathrm{loss}_i=q_i-C(\mathbf q)+C(\mathbf 0)$. Then
$\sup_{\mathbf q}\big(\langle e_i,\mathbf q\rangle - C(\mathbf q)\big)
=C^*(e_i)=R^{**}(e_i)=R(e_i)$ (Fenchel-Moreau, $R$ closed), and
$C(\mathbf 0)=\sup_p -R(p)=-\inf_p R(p)$; hence the supremum of the loss over
$\mathbf q$ is exactly $R(e_i)-\inf_p R(p)$. The final inequality holds
because $e_i\in\Delta$.

(iv) Lagrange: maximising $\langle p,\mathbf q\rangle-b\sum p_i\log p_i$
subject to $\sum p_i=1$ gives $q_i-b(\log p_i+1)=\lambda$, so
$p_i\propto e^{q_i/b}$, and substituting back yields
$C(\mathbf q)=b\log\sum_i e^{q_i/b}$. Then $R(e_i)=0$ and
$\inf R=-b\log n$ at the uniform distribution, so the loss bound is
$b\log n$. $\blacksquare$

Decentralised exchanges use a different design, the *constant-function
market maker* (CFMM). The pool holds reserves $r_1,r_2$ of two assets and
accepts any trade that leaves an invariant such as $r_1r_2=k$ unchanged
[@angeris2021uniswap; @angeris2023primer]. The two designs are convertible,
though not by the bare conjugacy of Theorem 2.

**Proposition 3 (cost-function markets and CFMMs are level-set duals).**
*Under the monotonicity, concavity, and reserve-domain hypotheses of
@frongillo2024axiomatic, cost-function prediction markets and
constant-function market makers can be converted into one another. In the
unconstrained-reserve sign convention a cost function $C$ gives a concave
CFMM potential by $\varphi(\mathbf r)=-C(-\mathbf r)$; bounded-reserve
versions require a perspective (level-set) construction. The equivalence is
a convex level-set duality; it is not the bare Fenchel conjugacy
$C\mapsto C^*$.*

@frongillo2024axiomatic give the general equivalence in full, and
@angeris2023primer and @angeris2021uniswap develop the CFMM side.

**Example (constant product).** Take two outcome tokens with reserves
$r_1,r_2$ and invariant $r_1r_2=k$. The pool's portfolio value at prices
$(p,1-p)$ is

$$V(p)=\inf\{p\,r_1+(1-p)\,r_2:\ r_1r_2= k\}
      =2\sqrt{k\,p(1-p)},$$

by the AM-GM inequality, with the infimum attained at
$r_1=\sqrt{k(1-p)/p}$, $r_2=\sqrt{kp/(1-p)}$. The value is largest, $\sqrt k$,
when the two outcomes are priced equally, and falls to zero as either price
goes to one. $V$ is concave, and reading $R(p)=-V(p)$ as the penalty of
Theorem 2 gives a maker whose worst-case loss is the range of $R$ on
$[0,1]$, namely $\sqrt k$, the geometric mean of the initial reserves. With
$k=100$ and reserves of $10$ and $10$, the pool is worth $10$ at even prices,
$6$ at prices $(0.9,0.1)$, and can lose at most $10$. The generator is not
entropic, which is why constant-product markets and the LMSR price the same
claims differently.

## 5. The two opinion pools

The organiser now holds forecasts $q_1,\dots,q_m$ with weights $w_i\ge0$,
$\sum_i w_i=1$, from stakes or track records, and wants one forecast. Two
averages are in common use. The *linear pool* is $\sum_i w_i q_i$
[@stone1961opinionpool; @bates1969combination]. The *logarithmic pool* is
proportional to $\prod_i q_i^{w_i}$, the weighted geometric mean,
renormalised to sum to one [@genest1986combining].

In the running example take $q_1=(0.5,0.3,0.2)$, $q_2=(0.2,0.3,0.5)$ and
equal weights. The linear pool is $(0.35,0.30,0.35)$ and the logarithmic
pool is $(0.339,0.322,0.339)$. Now replace $q_2$ by $(0,0.5,0.5)$, a
forecaster who rules $A$ out. The linear pool becomes $(0.25,0.40,0.35)$,
and the logarithmic pool becomes $(0,0.551,0.449)$. The linear pool keeps
any outcome that either forecaster finds likely; the logarithmic pool vetoes
any outcome that either forecaster rules out.

The two pools are the two senses of "closest to all the forecasts" under the
Kullback-Leibler divergence, which is not symmetric. The linear pool
minimises the divergence from each forecast to the average. The logarithmic
pool minimises the divergence from the average to each forecast. @abbas2009kl
gives this view of the two pools, with the weights as the decision maker's
assessment of each source.

**Proposition 4 (the linear and logarithmic pools are the two KL
barycenters).** *Let $q_1,\dots,q_m$ be densities with respect to a common
dominating measure, $w_i\ge0$, $\sum w_i=1$, and for the second display
assume $0<\int\prod_i q_i^{w_i}<\infty$. Then*

$$\textstyle\arg\min_p \sum_i w_i\,\mathrm{KL}(q_i\Vert p)=\sum_i w_i q_i,
\qquad
\arg\min_p \sum_i w_i\,\mathrm{KL}(p\Vert q_i)\ \propto\ \prod_i q_i^{w_i}.$$

**Proof.** For the first, $\sum_i w_i\,\mathrm{KL}(q_i\Vert p)
=\mathrm{const}-\int(\sum_i w_iq_i)\log p$, and $\int \bar q\log p$ is
maximized over densities at $p=\bar q$ (Gibbs). For the second,
$\sum_i w_i\,\mathrm{KL}(p\Vert q_i)=\int p\log p-\int p\,\overline{\log q}$
with $\overline{\log q}=\sum_i w_i\log q_i$; the Lagrange condition is
$\log p=\overline{\log q}+\mathrm{const}$. $\blacksquare$

Bayesian model averaging trains the weights by cumulative log score and then
mixes linearly, $\sum_m w_m F_m$: a linear pool with score-trained weights.
The logarithmic pool multiplies densities and renormalises. They are
different aggregates with different sharpness [@genest1986combining].

## 6. Merging market makers

Suppose two LMSR makers quote the running example side by side, one with
$b=10$ and one with $b=5$, and a trader wants $10$ shares of $A$. She splits
the order to minimise the total cost, sending $6.67$ shares to the deeper
maker and $3.33$ to the shallower one, in proportion to $b$, and pays
$4.12$. A single LMSR with $b=15$ charges $4.12$ for the same ten shares.
Two venues, optimally routed, are one venue with the liquidity added.

The reason is that the optimal split is an infimal convolution of the two
cost functions, and conjugation turns the infimal convolution of the costs
into the sum of the penalties.

**Proposition 5 (merging makers is infimal convolution;
@rockafellar1970convex, @bhaskara2023general).** *For closed proper convex
$f,g$ the conjugate identity $(f\,\square\,g)^*=f^*+g^*$ holds unconditionally;
recovering the primal form $f\,\square\,g=(f^*+g^*)^*$ needs $f\,\square\,g$
closed and the infimal convolution exact (automatic for the finite-valued
penalties here, since $\operatorname{ri}\operatorname{dom}R_1\cap
\operatorname{ri}\operatorname{dom}R_2=\operatorname{ri}\Delta\neq\varnothing$).
Consequently, merging two cost-function makers with penalties $R_1,R_2$
(cost functions $C_i=R_i^*$) yields the maker with penalty $R_1+R_2$, and
merging $\mathrm{LMSR}_{b_1}$ with $\mathrm{LMSR}_{b_2}$ yields
$\mathrm{LMSR}_{b_1+b_2}$: liquidity adds.*

**Proof.** $(f\,\square\,g)^*(p)
=\sup_x\langle p,x\rangle-\inf_y\{f(y)+g(x-y)\}
=\sup_{y,z}\langle p,y\rangle-f(y)+\langle p,z\rangle-g(z)
=f^*(p)+g^*(p)$. For the makers, $C_1\,\square\,C_2=(R_1+R_2)^*$ by
biconjugacy, and $b_1G+b_2G=(b_1+b_2)G$ for the entropic generator.
$\blacksquare$

The same identity is the composition law of the risk-sharing literature. The
aggregate of several agents' convex risk measures is their infimal
convolution, with the Pareto allocation as minimiser and the common
subgradient as the clearing price [@barrieu2005inf; @jouini2008optimal]. The
market-liquidity reading is developed by @bhaskara2023general.

## 7. Chaining mechanisms

**The common signature.** To chain mechanisms, each must accept what the
previous one produced. A *transducer* (Mealy machine) is a state machine
that reads an input stream and writes an output stream: a tuple
$(S,A,B,\delta,\lambda)$ with state space $S$, input alphabet $A$, output
alphabet $B$, transition map $\delta:S\times A\to S$, and output map
$\lambda:S\times A\to B$, run as $s_{t+1}=\delta(s_t,a_t)$ and
$b_t=\lambda(s_t,a_t)$. The mechanisms above share one instantiation. Let
$\mathrm{Dist}$ denote the set of distributional beliefs and take $S$ the
wealth states, $A=\mathrm{Dist}^m\times\mathcal X$ ($m$ participant reports
and, where the stage settles, a realised outcome), and
$B=\mathrm{Dist}\times\mathbb R^m$ (an aggregate belief and transfers).

A *stage* is such a transducer, written

$$M:\ (\mathrm{Dist}^m,\ w,\ x)\ \longmapsto\ (\mathrm{Dist},\ w',\ \pi).$$

A stage takes $m$ forecasts, the current wealths and possibly an outcome, and
returns one forecast, the new wealths and the payments.

The signature fixes what a stage consumes and emits, and nothing more. It
does not make the chain a proper mechanism: an upstream report can move a downstream stage's
settlement variable, its rewards, or the capital available to it, so a
report that maximises one stage's expected payment need not maximise the
total. The condition under which a chain is proper, an exogenous outcome
anchoring every stage, is the subject of the companion report
[@cotton2026multistage].

Compositional game theory [@ghani2018compositional] composes open games in sequence and in parallel
while carrying each player's best response and its dependence on the
surrounding game; the stages here carry beliefs and transfers but not best
responses, which is the difference between a wiring diagram and a game. A scoring rule is
the transfer component $\lambda$ of a stage, not itself a map
$\mathrm{Dist}\to\mathrm{Dist}$. A market maker is a stage whose state is
the inventory vector and whose emitted belief is the price. An opinion pool
is a stage with no outcome argument and zero transfers. Composition wires
the belief output of one stage to the belief inputs of the next while state
and transfers thread through.

The operators below act on stages.

**Sequentialise.** Theorem 2: a proper score run sequentially against a
wealth state is a cost-function market maker. The LMSR is the logarithmic
score sequentialised.

**Pool.** A proper score gives a batch elicitation mechanism when reports are
scored independently and funded externally: properness is inherited report by
report. Parimutuel and budget-balanced versions are a different game, because
the pot split couples payoffs through the denominator. The price-taking
analysis [@cotton2026pointcloud, §2] gives truthful all-in, a symmetric
equilibrium at fractional stakes, and degeneracy as the stake fraction
vanishes, and beyond that the equilibrium theory is open.

**Ensemble.** Proposition 4: the linear and logarithmic pools, applied to
the belief outputs of several stages.

**Merge.** Proposition 5: two makers in parallel are one maker with the
penalties added.

**Serial composition.** A joint model is a factorisation,
$P(\text{everything})=\prod_i P(x_i\mid\text{parents})$, and the serial
arrangement runs one venue per factor, each pricing its conditional given
what is upstream and settling in cascade. The locality that makes this
tradable is Hanson's modularity: in a combinatorial logarithmic market
scoring rule a bet on $A\mid B$ moves that conditional and nothing else,
uniquely among market scoring rules
[@hanson2003combinatorial; @hanson2007logarithmic]. Pricing a combinatorial
market is probabilistic inference, which is why exact LMSR pricing over a
combinatorial space is #P-hard [@chen2008complexity] and why a deployed
combinatorial market ran its updates on the junction-tree algorithm
[@sun2012junction]. @pennock1996marketbayes map a Bayes net to an economy
with one agent per conditional-probability entry and show that equilibrium
prices equal the network's probabilities.

Parallel merge and serial composition are the two operations of a
commutative semiring, the setting of the generalised distributive law
[@aji2000gdl]. Assign each factor the potential $\varphi_i=-\log p_i$.
Parallel merge adds potentials, which is the conjugate statement of
Proposition 5, and serial composition is the min-plus kernel product
$\inf_y[\varphi_1(x,y)+\varphi_2(y,z)]$. A market of optimising traders
therefore computes min-plus: a chain of stage potentials prices the Viterbi
decoding of the corresponding hidden Markov model. On log-quadratic
families partial minimisation equals marginalisation up to a constant, by
the Schur-complement identity, so there the alternation of a serial step
with a parallel merge reproduces the Kalman filter [@kalman1960filtering]
exactly. Off that family a market prices the max-marginal rather than the
marginal.

Both identities, the Viterbi decoding by routing and the Kalman filter by
alternating a model step with a market step, are checked to
machine precision in
[`mechanisms/serial_markets.py`](../mechanisms/serial_markets.py) and
[`tests/test_serial_markets.py`](../tests/test_serial_markets.py).

**Transform.** Run a stage in a transformed coordinate and map back. Whether
propriety survives depends on whether the transformation depends on the
forecast.

- *Fixed transformations.* Properness is preserved under any fixed
  transformation of forecast and outcome, and strict propriety iff the
  transformation is injective [@allen2023transformed, Prop. 4;
  @pic2025proper, Prop. 1]. The Markov-kernel (stochastic channel) extension,
  strict propriety iff the channel is injective on laws, is Theorem 2 of the
  point-cloud paper [@cotton2026pointcloud], whose Theorem 1 also exhibits
  the canonical failure: a kernel-density smoothing seam whose raw-outcome
  score elicits a deconvolution.
- *Forecast-dependent transformations.* The probability integral transform
  below transforms outcomes by the reported $F$ itself, so the
  fixed-transformation theorems do not apply to it. It is a calibration
  diagnostic rather than a strictly proper score. The stacked-lottery design
  [@cotton2020lottery, slides 29-31] is this operator in practice:
  percentiles from one game feed the next, and calibration is produced by
  composing monotone maps contributed by competing algorithms.

**The probability integral transform.** A forecaster who reports a
distribution function $F$ for a continuous outcome $X$ has, if the report is
right, made $U=F(X)$ uniform on $(0,1)$. Suppose instead the report is a
standard normal and the truth is normal with standard deviation $2$. The
event $U<0.025$, which should have probability $0.025$, has probability
$0.164$, and the middle half of the unit interval receives $0.264$ instead of
$0.5$. A stage downstream can detect the departure without knowing the true
law.

**Proposition 6 (the probability integral transform;
@rosenblatt1952remarks, @dawid1984prequential).** *If $X$ has continuous CDF
$F$ then $U=F(X)\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$, and $z=\Phi^{-1}(U)\sim N(0,1)$.
In the prequential setting, if $F_t$ is the true conditional law of $X_t$
given the past, then $U_t=F_t(X_t)$ is conditionally uniform and the PIT
stream is iid uniform.*

**Proof.** For continuous $F$, with the generalized inverse
$F^{-}(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge u\}$, the event $\{F(X)\le u\}$ differs from
$\{X\le F^{-}(u)\}$ by a set of probability zero, and
$\Pr(X\le F^{-}(u))=F(F^{-}(u))=u$ by continuity. The prequential statement
applies this conditionally at each $t$. $\blacksquare$

The converse fails. Reporting the unconditional law $F$ of an iid sequence
gives $F(X_t)\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ even if valuable covariates were
ignored, so marginally uniform PITs do not certify an informative forecast.
A PIT critic witnesses miscalibration relative to its test class; it
complements, and does not replace, a proper score that rewards sharp
conditional distributions. Split-conformal prediction depends on this
distinction. For discrete forecasts the
randomized PIT preserves the exact uniform null, while the mid-PIT is a
convenient deterministic diagnostic with a different null distribution.

## 8. Clamped mechanisms

Between a full ecosystem, in which every stage is a live venue with free
entry, and a single fitted model, there is a continuum of *clamped*
mechanisms: the same composition with some degree of freedom frozen.
Ordinary statistical procedures are at the clamped end. Each applies one
clamp, and each clamp forfeits a quantity that can be named.

**Freeze entry: Bayesian model averaging.** A market of Kelly bettors prices
the wealth-weighted average of its participants' beliefs, and the wealth
updates are Bayes updates, so the market performs Bayesian model averaging
with wealths as posterior weights
[@kelly1956newinterpretation; @breiman1961optimal; @beygelzimer2012kelly].
In the running example two bettors with equal wealth hold
$q_1=(0.5,0.3,0.2)$ and $q_2=(0.2,0.3,0.5)$, and the market quotes their
linear pool $(0.35,0.30,0.35)$. If $A$ occurs the wealths become
$0.714$ and $0.286$, the posterior weights under an equal prior, and the
next quote is $0.714\,q_1+0.286\,q_2$. Model averaging over a fixed model
list is this market with entry closed, and the clamp forfeits whatever a
model outside the list would have earned [@blume2006smart].

**Freeze capital: least squares.** Precision-weighted estimation of a common
mean is a merge of quadratic makers, one per observation, each quoting its
value with capital equal to its precision. Two observations, $1.0$ with
variance $1$ and $2.0$ with variance $1/4$, merge to the estimate $1.8$ with
precision $5$: precisions add because liquidity adds (Proposition 5).
Fixing the capitals at the nominal precisions is the clamp. The market
version lets a source that has been wrong lose capital, which is the
difference between weighted least squares and its adaptive variants.

**Freeze the fee: frictionless aggregation.** A maker with no fee earns
nothing on uninformed flow and cannot recover adverse-selection losses from
volume. Setting the fee to zero turns a venue into an aggregation rule.
Letting each maker quote its own fee turns the spread into a price, and the
aggregate of fee-bearing makers is a consolidated limit order book
[@cotton2026nonconvex; @cotton2026bounded].

**Freeze propagation: the Kalman filter.** In the filtering recursion the
correction step is a parallel merge, executed by trades against an
observation maker, while the prediction step is computed by whoever owns
the dynamics. Nobody is paid to move the state forward. Unclamping means
posting the transition as a venue with securities on the pair
$(x_t,x_{t+1})$, which requires a settlement rule for that venue, and
there is no general theorem that self-interested trading performs the
elimination.

**Freeze the residual venue: split-conformal prediction.** Split-conformal
prediction fits a point predictor on one half of the data, computes the
absolute residuals on the other half, and reports the prediction plus or
minus the 90th percentile of those residuals [@lei2018distribution]. The
interval covers 90 percent of new outcomes, averaged over inputs, with no
assumption on the predictor. As a chain, this is a base predictor feeding a
residual stage whose field is restricted to a single *unconditional* entry:
one residual law, applied at every input.

In a log-wealth pool settling on the residual, an entrant who conditions on
the input $X$ out-earns the unconditional entry at the rate $I(R;X)$, the
mutual information between residual and input, which in the Gaussian case
is $-\tfrac12\log(1-\rho^2)$ [@cotton2026conformalbetting]. That rate is
the rent the clamp forfeits. Marginal coverage is the break-even statement
of the clamped venue: the unconditional entry is priced correctly on
average, so it is safe, and the conditional information is unpriced. The gap does not close when the base forecast is
calibrated, because marginal correctness is not conditional correctness
[@barber2021limits]. When the residual stage is run as an actual pool the
rent is collected; the mechanism ran in production as the microprediction
residual streams and the MidOne contest [@cotton2026multistage].

**The unclamped end.** In a nearest-the-pin parimutuel over a continuum,
participants submit clouds of samples, the pot is split in proportion to
the density each placed at the realised outcome, and entry is open; this
was the reward engine behind monteprediction [@cotton2024monteprediction].
Who enters, how much each stakes, what each conditions on, and how sharp a
submission is are all unclamped. Open entry brings its own design problems:
scoring a kernel density at the raw outcome elicits a deconvolution of the
belief rather than the belief [@cotton2026pointcloud].

Each clamp replaces a price with an assumption:

| clamp | assumption replacing a price | forfeited |
|---|---|---|
| entry closed | the model list is adequate | what an outside model would earn |
| capital fixed | nominal precisions are right | the correction from realised performance |
| fee zero | flow is uninformed | adverse-selection revenue |
| propagation computed | the dynamics are known | the price of the transition |
| residual unconditional | covariates carry nothing | $I(R;X)$ |

Only the last entry has a closed form. Unclamping a stage requires a
settlement rule for that stage's securities, and a latent quantity with no
settlement functional is not a market.

## 9. Implementation notes

The mechanisms are implemented against a single interface patterned on the
skaters time-series contract [@cotton_skaters], a successor to timemachines
[@cotton_timemachines]: every stage consumes and emits the same
distributional type and threads its own state, so the stage signature
is the forecasting contract with wealth in place of model state. The
scoring rules are in
[`mechanisms/scoring_rules.py`](../mechanisms/scoring_rules.py), the LMSR in
[`mechanisms/lmsr.py`](../mechanisms/lmsr.py), and the two pools in
[`mechanisms/aggregation.py`](../mechanisms/aggregation.py). The chained
elicitation-then-calibration pipeline runs in
[`examples/sim_pipeline.py`](../examples/sim_pipeline.py), and every number
quoted for the running example is reproduced by
[`examples/primer_numbers.py`](../examples/primer_numbers.py). Scores are
implemented in loss form, with the sign reversed from the reward form.
